extracted.intended_audience: researchers in cognitive neuroscience, social cognition, and autism (fMRI researchers)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, analysing, and reporting an fMRI experiment that compares neural responses to different types of laughter (spontaneous vs conversational) and control vocalizations in autistic and non-autistic adults using whole-brain and ROI approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent ROI definition / avoid circular analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt an independent approach for hypothesis testing so that the data used to define ROIs are not related to the hypothesis-testing data (cites Kriegeskorte et al. 2009). Example: use MNI peak coordinates from a prior fMRI study to define ROIs (e.g., McGettigan et al. 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define ROIs from prior studies or independent meta-analyses to avoid 'double dipping'; this preserves valid null-hypothesis testing and maximizes statistical power to detect group differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an appropriate control condition (noise-vocoded human vocalization, NV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast laughter conditions against a high-level acoustic baseline (NV = noise-vocoded human vocalization) to isolate laughter-related activity while controlling for low-level sound and speech processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include control stimuli that preserve some acoustic complexity (e.g., noise-vocoded speech) so activation in auditory and higher-order regions reflects laughter/humor processing rather than simple acoustic differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whole-brain analysis with correction and ROI follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform whole-brain analyses with appropriate multiple-comparisons correction and then use ROI analyses (predefined independently) to test prior hypotheses (e.g., mPFC, thalamus, ACC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report whole-brain-corrected results and then conduct targeted ROI tests for hypothesis-driven contrasts; note where whole-brain clusters do or do not show group differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of ROIs from prior literature and meta-analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose ROIs based on coordinates reported in prior studies (e.g., McGettigan et al. 2015) or meta-analytic results (e.g., Van Overwalle 2009) to target networks such as mentalizing (mPFC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide MNI coordinates and references for each ROI used; justify ROI choices by linking to relevant prior empirical or meta-analytic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical design and full reporting (ANOVA, follow-ups, effect sizes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate factorial designs (e.g., 3 (ROIs) × 2 (Contrasts) × 2 (Groups) ANOVA) and report F-statistics, degrees of freedom, p-values, and effect sizes (e.g., eta-squared); conduct and report follow-up tests (t-tests) with Cohen's d and means/SEMs/SDs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present complete inferential statistics for omnibus tests and post-hoc comparisons (including effect sizes and descriptive statistics) to support claims about group and condition effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report activation tables with coordinates, cluster sizes, and test statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide tables listing significant brain regions with number of voxels, MNI coordinates (x,y,z), and test statistics (T, Z) for contrasts (e.g., Table 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear tables for whole-brain results (voxels, coordinates, peak T/Z values) to allow interpretation and comparison with prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: FIR event-related time-course analysis parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: When unpacking temporal dynamics, extract finite impulse response (FIR) time-courses with specified length and bin size (example: FIR length 30 sec, time bins 3 s) across trials of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify FIR window length and bin width, and plot average time series with error bars; use FIR to detect delayed integration effects (e.g., later responses in SMA and precuneus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify ROI extraction geometry (sphere size)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the spatial extent for ROI signal extraction (example: SMA MNI peak coordinate with an 8 mm sphere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report sphere radii or mask definitions used for extracting mean signal so analyses are reproducible and comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select time-course ROIs based on prior whole-brain interest and literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose regions for time-course analyses informed by whole-brain results and prior studies (example regions: bilateral HG, STG, SMA, bilateral precuneus), motivated by their roles in auditory, laughter, and humor processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground selection of temporal-ROI targets in prior empirical findings to justify focusing on those nodes for hemodynamic time-course comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use implicit experimental manipulations to prevent compensatory strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ cover stories and implicit tasks (e.g., presenting words plus laughter with a cover story about a comedian) to measure spontaneous/implicit processing rather than explicit judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit designs can prevent participants, especially clinical groups, from using compensatory cognitive strategies and better index naturalistic processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish laughter processing from humor processing in design
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that designs that pair laughter with words may not disentangle neural processing of laughter per se from processing of humor; the present design does not separate these components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claiming to study laughter-specific mechanisms vs humor, include manipulations that isolate each component or use modalities/temporal resolutions (e.g., MEG) that can dissociate their time courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect baseline behavioral measures (e.g., baseline funniness ratings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain baseline measures for stimuli (e.g., funniness ratings of words) from all participant groups to support interpretation of modulation effects; omission is a noted limitation in this study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include baseline behavioral data so neural modulation by laughter can be interpreted relative to pre-existing stimulus ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for sensitivity to background noise and testing modality
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that implicit auditory effects can be highly sensitive to background noise and that this may preclude some testing modalities (e.g., online testing was precluded here due to noise sensitivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control acoustic environment in in-lab studies or carefully design online audio protocols; report limitations when constraints affect data collection options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret non-auditory activations (e.g., primary visual cortex) as potential imagery or higher-order processes
rubrics_metrics.description: When visual cortex or other non-stimulated regions are recruited in auditory paradigms, consider interpretations such as visual imagery, metacognition, autobiographical memory, or default mode involvement (e.g., precuneus, PCC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss plausible cognitive mechanisms (visual imagery, reflective/metacognitive processes) for unexpected activations and link to literature (precuneus, PCC roles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report and discuss limitations and real-world implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state study limitations (e.g., inability to collect baseline ratings, inability to distinguish laughter vs humor) and discuss implications (e.g., autistic people may face challenges understanding conversational laughter; recommend clearer communication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclude with balanced interpretation, noting ecological/clinical implications and suggestions for future research or practice.
